title: From 36% to 100%: How Self-Improving Agents Write Their Own Skills — Rafal Wilinski, Runlayer
talk_summary: Rafal Wilinski argues that agents should distill successful and failed run traces into reusable 'skills' (playbooks) stored in a central library and served via an MCP gateway, so one agent's hard-won solution becomes every agent's starting point. He cites a Chromium-in-Lambda task going from 36% to 100% success after a single distilled skill was added, and frames the flywheel as a moat against rented/deprecating frontier intelligence.

takeaways.technique: Distill skills from run traces (success and failure)
takeaways.what_they_do: When a run succeeds with many tool calls, or fails in an interesting way, they take the trace and ask a frontier model to distill a reusable skill/playbook; failures expose missing guardrails and edge cases, successes validate the skill.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we just take that trace and we ask Frontier LM to simply distill a skill
takeaways.numbers: 36% -> 100% success rate on Chromium-in-AWS-Lambda task with Sonnet 4.6

takeaways.technique: Central skill library as organizational memory
takeaways.what_they_do: Skills land in a governed central library that is continuously updated, so knowledge from one agent's run is available to all agents and clients instead of dying with the session.
takeaways.evidence_quote: once one agent figure outs a really hard problem, it's getting distilled into a skill persistent in all or organizational library

takeaways.what_they_do: Instead of local skill files per client, they run a remote MCP server as the source of truth; clients search for relevant skills and the server enforces policy and serves the best version per role/query.
takeaways.evidence_quote: instead of installing skills locally, you can create a remote MCP server which can become the source of truth across your whole company

takeaways.what_they_do: Distilled skills pass a series of automated checks (prompt injection, PII, other) before landing in the library; they also scan third-party skills and find malicious content.
takeaways.evidence_quote: it passes through our various series of checks like whether it's not containing some kind of prompt injection or maybe PII

takeaways.what_they_do: A good skill reduces branching and tool calls, so agents explore fewer dead ends and spend fewer tokens and dollars per task.
takeaways.evidence_quote: good skill is narrowing the search space ... stops doing tool calls and it's exploring less branches

takeaways.technique: Use frontier model to persist procedures before it's gone
takeaways.what_they_do: While access to the best model exists, use it to discover and persist procedures into skills, making the org resilient to model deprecation or degradation.
takeaways.evidence_quote: while we have the access to the best version of that intelligence, we should be using that to discover and persist those use useful procedures
